# Issue #1518: yaml: a round trip that keeps comments and layout — which edit model?

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1518).

`decision`, `yaml` · opened 2026-11-09 · updated 2026-11-09 · 1 comment

Part of #928. Builds on the writer (#1515).

## Where the question comes from

The owner wants full round trips: read a YAML file, change a value, write it back, and keep the comments, key order, indentation, quoting and blank lines. Today the parser drops comments (`rule Comment = "#" until("\n" | eof) -> { }` in `packages/yaml/src/main.nika`) and no node keeps its span or style. ADR-yaml-1 D10 lists "format-preserving editing (comments, order, indentation kept)" as a later stage that needs "the tree carrying comments and every token's span; an ADR of its own for the edit model". This is that ADR's question. It is not obvious: there are several consistent designs that differ in cost, in API and in what "kept" means.

## Alternatives

**0. Do nothing.** The package reads and (after #1515) writes canonically, the way serde_yaml does.
* For: no work, small tree.
* Against: config tools (Kubernetes manifests, CI files, Ansible) need edit-in-place; without it users reach for ruamel.yaml or hand-written regex. The showcase would fall short of the owner's goal.

**1. Lossless syntax tree** (rust-analyzer's rowan, Swift's libSyntax): every token, including whitespace and comments, is a node; the typed `Node` tree is a view over it.
* For: byte identity by construction; any edit, even inside a flow collection, keeps everything around it.
* Against: two trees, a second API to learn, much more memory per document; a large change to a parser that builds its tree in grammar actions.

**2. Comments as trivia on nodes, re-rendered** (ruamel.yaml's round-trip mode, Go `yaml.v3` `HeadComment`/`LineComment`/`FootComment`): nodes carry their comments and style; the writer renders the whole tree.
* For: one tree, simple API, comments survive edits.
* Against: not byte-identical: indentation of sequences, spacing, line folding and blank lines get normalised. ruamel.yaml's users know these diffs well.

**3. Spans and decor, copy what is untouched** (toml_edit, Cargo's way of editing `Cargo.toml`): every node keeps its source span, its style and the comments/whitespace around it ("decor"). The writer copies an unchanged node's bytes from the source and renders only changed or new nodes, in the style and indentation of their neighbours.
* For: parse-then-write is byte-identical; an edit changes only the lines it touches; one tree with a few extra fields; reuses #1515's emitter for new nodes; proven in the Rust ecosystem.
* Against: the tree must keep the source alive (or a copy); rules for "style of the neighbours" need care; nodes created by `merge`/anchors need a defined rendering.

## Other languages

* Python: ruamel.yaml (2), PyYAML drops comments (0).
* Go: yaml.v3 (2).
* Rust: serde_yaml / saphyr drop comments (0); toml_edit does (3) for TOML.
* JavaScript: `yaml` (eemeli) keeps comments on nodes and re-renders (2).

## Recommendation

**3, spans and decor.** It is the only one of the cheaper designs that gives byte identity, and byte identity is what "full round trip" means to a user diffing a file under version control. 1 gives the same guarantee at a much higher price in memory and API.

If decided so, the build:
1. `Node` gains `span` and `decor` (leading comments/blank lines, trailing comment), the parser fills them (grammar rules return the comments instead of discarding them).
2. `yaml::write_preserving(doc)` copies unchanged spans and renders changed nodes with #1515's emitter in the neighbours' style.
3. Done when: every yaml-test-suite input parses and writes back byte-identical, and a set of edit tests (change a scalar, add a key, remove an item, under comments) diff only in the edited lines.
4. The facade gets no new surface (serde_yaml has none for this); the Nikaia API is the showcase.

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-11-09](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1518#issuecomment-6752466479)

#### Additions to alternative 3 (from an outside review and the owner)

These sharpen the recommendation; they do not change it.

**1. One source, spans are numbers.** The edit document owns exactly one `Bytes`, the source. Every node keeps its span as two byte offsets into it; `write_preserving` copies untouched ranges straight from that source to the output. Scalar text stays a view into the source as today (Part III, `bulk text is a tethered slice`): while the document lives, the source is held anyway, so a view costs nothing extra. A value taken out of the document and kept after it is the language's ordinary case: the tether keeps the whole buffer, the compiler warns and suggests `.clone()` (Part III, *Retention*, ADR-283 D6). No separate "detach from source" operation: `.clone()` is that operation, until a measurement shows otherwise.

**2. The parser takes `Bytes`.** Then `fs::map` (a `Mapped` is a `Bytes`) and `fs::read` both go in without a copy. No new memory abstraction.

**3. Writing back never overwrites the source in place.** A document read from `fs::map(p)` and written to `p` would overwrite the pages it is still copying from. `write_preserving` to a path writes a new file beside it and renames it over the old one; a test covers map-then-write-to-same-path.

**4. Only who writes back pays: two entry points, one grammar.**
* `yaml::parse` stays lean as today: no spans, no decor, comments dropped. The serde facade uses it.
* A second entry (name to be fixed in the build, e.g. `yaml::edit`) returns the edit document that `write_preserving` takes.
* Both run the same grammar. A grammar parameter (grammar values, #932) switches whether comment and blank-line rules collect decor or discard it as `Comment` does now. No second parser that can drift.

#### Measurement before the build fixes the tree shape

Per `docs/measuring.md` (callgrind instruction counts, never time; against tuned Rust):
* **What:** the cost of spans alone, and of spans plus decor, on the lean read path.
* **How:** build a probe variant of `Node` with the two offsets filled in, and one that also collects decor. Count with callgrind on the yaml-test-suite inputs and on the large inputs of `benches/yaml` (#1517): `yaml::parse` without and with each addition. Report peak heap (massif or the allocator count) beside it.
* **Decision rule:** if spans cost under 2 % instructions and under 5 % heap on the lean path, one `Node` type carries spans always, and only decor hangs on the mode. Otherwise spans also live only in the edit document. The numbers and the chosen shape go into the ADR for the edit model.

#### Updated build (if decided as recommended)
1. Measurement above; result and chosen shape in the ADR.
2. Grammar parameter for decor; `Node` (or the edit node) gains `span` and `decor` per the measurement; the parser takes `Bytes`.
3. The edit entry point and `yaml::write_preserving`: copies untouched spans, renders changed nodes with #1515's emitter in the neighbours' style, writes to a new file and renames.
4. Done when: every yaml-test-suite input parses and writes back byte-identical through the edit entry; edit tests (change a scalar, add a key, remove an item, under comments) differ only in the edited lines; the map-then-write-same-path test passes; `yaml::parse` instruction counts in `benches/yaml` are unchanged within the measured rule.

- The two-scalar lowering (D2) is filed as its own issue, or this issue names why not (the count).

---

<details><summary>ADR-failure-return-1 text</summary>

## ADR-failure-return-1: A Failure's Status Travels Beside the Value, and the Throw Path Is Cold

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** November 9, 2026
**Answers:** ADR-023 §3.1 (where the success/failure decision lives), and how
ADR-023 D10's "the success path pays no memory round trip" is kept on each
backend
**Supersedes / Related:**
[ADR-023](adr-023.md) D10 (the cost guarantee; made precise here), §3.1
(answered here), §4 (the literal carry flag; reopened for one backend);
[ADR-280](adr-280.md) D24, D25 (the one-word tail whose non-zero word this
uses), §6 (in-value versus out-of-band status; answered here);
[ADR-283](adr-283.md) (views, the two-word return this cares about);
[ADR-004](adr-004.md) (the Rust backend);
issue #1235 (our own optimiser, Cranelift, copy-and-patch);
`docs/measuring.md`

## 1. Question

ADR-023 D10 promises, normatively, that a call which can fail pays no memory
round trip on success. ADR-023 §3.1 left open how: the status **in the value**
(A, a tag in a niche, what Rust gives) or **beside it** (B, a register of its
own, for a backend that owns its calling convention). Issue #1235 plans exactly
such a backend. So the question is no longer theoretical, and it has to be
measured against what the Rust backend actually does today.

## 2. What was measured

`nikaia-std` as it stands, `rustc 1.97`, `opt-level = 3`, x86-64, callgrind;
the functions `#[inline(never)]` so the call boundary is visible. The shapes
are what `nikaia lower` writes for `fn one(n: i64) -> i64 throws` and its
neighbours.

| Return on success | Size | Comes back in | Callee instructions |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Result<i64, Thrown<Kind>>` (fieldless error) | 16 B | memory (sret) | 10 |
| `Result<i64, Thrown<Code>>` (`Code(u64)`) | 16 B | memory (sret) | 13 |
| `Result<(), Thrown<Kind>>` | 16 B | registers | – |
| `Result<&str, Thrown<Kind>>`, `Result<(i64, i64), …>` | 24 B | memory (sret) | – |
| pair `(i64, usize)`: second word 0 = success, else the tail word | 16 B | registers | 5 |

Findings:

* **Today ADR-023 D10 holds for no failing call that returns a value.** The tag
  sits in the error's own byte, and Rust returns such an enum through memory
  even at 16 bytes. `crates/nikaia-std/src/error.rs` asserts the size, not the
  way it is returned.
* **The two-scalar pair** saves 4 instructions a call net (21.4 M against
  17.4 M over 10⁶ calls) and the whole memory round trip.
* **`throwing` is not cold.** For `Thrown<Code>` LLVM inlines the trace
  machinery, and every call, failing or not, pays two pushes and a 168-byte
  frame (13 against 10 instructions).
* **Cranelift with its own convention (`tail`)** returns pointer, length and
  status in `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`; the caller is `call; test; jnz`, no memory.
  With System V the status goes to memory.
* **An inlined call has no ABI.** Everything above concerns calls LLVM does not
  inline: across crates without LTO, recursion, large functions. How common
  those are in real programs is **not measured yet**.

## 3. Options

* **A as it is**: keep `Result<T, Thrown<E>>`. Breaks ADR-023 D10 as measured.
* **A with a two-scalar lowering**: in-value status, but written by the
  lowering as two plain words Rust returns in registers. Holds ADR-023 D10 for
  `T` up to one word; cannot hold it for a two-word `T`.
* **B, a status register**: on a backend that owns its convention. Holds
  ADR-023 D10 for `T` up to two words.
* **B in the carry flag**: one register and one instruction fewer than B on
  x86-64; reachable only where the throw and check sequences are hand-written.

## 4. Decision

### D1 — The throw path is cold, and the failing function stays inlinable.

`throwing` and every constructor of an envelope on the throw path are
`#[cold]` and `#[inline(never)]`. A function that can fail is **not** kept from
inlining: its body shrinks to a compare, a branch and a cold call, which makes
it a better inlining candidate, and an inlined call has no return convention
to pay for at all.

A test checks the code a failing call compiles to, not only its size: a
non-failing call to `fn one(n: i64) -> i64 throws` touches no stack memory.

### D2 — On the Rust backend, a failing call returns two scalars where the value and the error fit one word each.

Where `T` fits one word and `E`'s payload fits one word, the lowering writes
`(T-or-payload, tail)` instead of `Result<T, Thrown<E>>`. The tail word is
never zero (ADR-280 D25); zero is success. A crossing into Rust code the
program did not lower converts back to `Result` in a shim, which ADR-023 §3.1
already counts as ordinary at a boundary.

Built only after the measurement in §6 shows non-inlined failing calls carry
real weight in our programs and benchmarks.

### D3 — ADR-023 D10 is stated per backend.

ADR-023 D10's guarantee reads: **on the Rust backend**, a failing call
returning a value of up to one word pays no memory round trip; a two-word
value (a view, a pair) does, until the direct backend exists. **On the direct
backend**, the guarantee holds up to two words. The gap is named, not hidden.

### D4 — On the direct backend, the status is a register of its own (ADR-023 §3.1: B).

The Nikaia-internal calling convention of the direct path in issue #1235
returns the status beside the value, in a register: in Cranelift a further
return value under its own convention. The value keeps every return register
it would have without `throws`. Calls to and from Rust and C use their
conventions and meet through a shim; a program of Nikaia and `std` only has no
such boundary.

### D5 — The carry flag is a measurement, not a decision.

ADR-023 §4 rejected the carry flag because no backend we used could reach it.
Copy-and-patch can: the two sequences involved (`stc; ret` and `jc` after the
call) are short enough to write by hand as stencils, and nothing between `ret`
and `jc` touches the flags. A successful return then needs `clc` unless the
last flag write is known to leave carry clear (`xor`, `test`, an unsigned
operation proven or checked not to overflow).

The prototype in issue #1235, step 7, measures it against D4's register on the
same kernels. It is adopted on x86-64 only if it gains measurably; ARM64 and
RISC-V keep the register.

## 5. Reasons

* **The guarantee was not met, and nobody saw it**, because the test checks
  size, not convention. D1's test closes that.
* **D1 costs nothing and helps inlining.** The common small failing function
  gets faster by being inlined, which is better than any return convention.
* **D2 is the most Rust can give.** A two-word `T` plus a status is three
  words; Rust's convention has two registers for it. Only B gets past that.
* **D4 follows from issue #1235.** Designing the direct path's convention
  without the status would mean redesigning it later.
* **D5 keeps the question honest.** callgrind counts instructions, not µops;
  `test` and `jnz` fuse on current cores, so the carry flag's real gain is a
  register and perhaps nothing more. Only a measured prototype says.

## 6. Open

* **How many failing calls are not inlined** in our programs (the compiler
  through `lower-std`, the benchmarks, `tools/*.nika`), counted as
  `docs/measuring.md` says. Gates D2.
* **The carry flag against the register**, issue #1235, step 7. Decides D5.
* **Whether the ledger narrows a call site's set to empty** where a proof makes
  the only `throw` unreachable; such a call could take the plain convention.

## 7. Considered and rejected

* **Forbidding inlining of failing functions.** It would put every small
  failing call back across a return convention, the one place the cost lives.
* **A as it is, ADR-023 D10 unchanged.** A normative guarantee that is not met
  is worse than a precise one that is.
* **The carry flag on Cranelift or LLVM.** Neither models a flag across a
  call; D4's register is their form of B.
* **A wider pair (three scalars) on the Rust backend.** Rust returns three
  words through memory; nothing is gained over today.

## 8. Consequences

* `crates/nikaia-std/src/error.rs`: `#[cold]` and `#[inline(never)]` on the
  throw-path constructors; a test on the compiled call, beside the size
  assertions.
* ADR-023: D10 rewritten per D3; §3.1 marked answered; §4's carry-flag entry
  points to D5.
* ADR-280 §6: the in-value versus out-of-band question marked answered.
* Issue #1235: the direct path's convention carries the status register (D4);
  step 7 adds the carry-flag measurement (D5).
* After §6's count: the two-scalar lowering (D2), with shims at Rust crossings.

</details>

# Issue #1533: http: the body rate counts from the body's first byte (ADR-326 D7)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1533).

`libraries`, `ready`, `wip` · opened 2026-11-10 · updated 2026-11-10 · 0 comments

**Governing decision:** [ADR-326](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-326.md) D7: "The rate is the bytes so far over the time since the body's first byte".

## What is wrong today

The build for #1526 (6b954db6) starts the body's clock when the head ends (`let body_started = time::now()` in `request`, `examples/http/src/main.nika` ~410). A client that sends the head and waits before the first body byte has that wait counted against its rate. D7 counts from the first body byte. The wait before it belongs to D8's per-read deadline.

## To build

1. Start `body_started` when the first body byte is in the buffer: the bytes that came with the head, or else the first read after the head. Do not start it at the head's end.
2. A test in `tests/compiler/` beside `http_listen_times_out_a_slow_head_and_body`: a client sends the head, waits longer than the start-up period, then sends the body at full speed, and is answered `200`.

## Done when

The test passes, and `http_listen_times_out_a_slow_head_and_body` still gives `408` for a body sent a byte at a time.

## Files

`examples/http/src/main.nika`, `tests/compiler/http_listen_*`.

## Out of scope

The read deadline itself (D8). The run for #1526 built it on the poller's deadline instead of racing `time::sleep_until`, with the same behaviour, and the supervisor accepted that.

# Issue #1548: yaml: close the gap to saphyr-parser found by benches/yaml (events 2.8x on large, 5.4x on deep)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1548).

`blocked`, `yaml` · opened 2026-11-10 · updated 2026-11-10 · 5 comments

Filed by the driver from the `Found:` of the run of `issue-1517` (#1517); rewritten by the supervisor (2026-11-10).

## Found

`benches/yaml` (#1517) counts `yaml::events` with checks off at 2.82x the instructions of saphyr-parser on the 10 MB input, 5.41x on `deep`, 2.78x on `scalars` and 3.37x on the suite cases. The callgrind profile names five causes (repro: `nikaia run benches/yaml/bench.nika -- 1`, then `callgrind_annotate` on `target/yaml-bench/bin/events.off inputs/large.yaml`):

1. **Events are copied once per nesting level.** The walk (`walk`/`events` in packages/yaml/src) returns a `Vec[Event]` per node and the parent extends it. Grow and extend take 42 % of `yaml::events` on `deep`.
2. **The grammar threads `ds: Vec[Dir]` through every node rule and clones it per call.** `List<Dir>::clone_in` takes 5 % of `large`, where the list is empty.
3. **Rule `Props` tries `Tag(ds)` in two alternatives on every node.** `parse_Tag` and `parse_Props` take 10 % of `large`.
4. **malloc, free and memcpy take 23 % of `large`.** There is a String per scalar, and the events are built from the Node tree rather than streamed.
5. **Plain scalars are read per character** (`parse_PlainChar`, `list::chars`): 9 % of `large`.

## To build

Each cause is its own commit, measured with callgrind before and after (`docs/measuring.md`):

- [ ] 1: the walk writes into one output `Vec[Event]` passed down, or streams; no per-level copy.
- [ ] 2: `ds` is passed by reference (a view) or kept in the parser's state, not cloned per rule call.
- [ ] 3: `Props` parses a tag once (factor the common prefix of the two alternatives).
- [ ] 4: events come straight from the parse, not via the Node tree; a scalar is a span of the input until a String is asked for. Keep in step with the span design of #1518.
- [ ] 5: a run of plain characters is matched as a run (a byte loop or a `Mask` scan, as in `benches/brc/fast.nika`), not one rule call per character.
- [ ] A cause that cannot be fixed in the package (a compiler or grammar-codegen defect) is fixed there with a test in `tests/compiler/`, per CLAUDE.md.
- [ ] Re-run `benches/yaml/bench.nika` and update the table and the causes in `benches/yaml/README.md`.

## Done when

- `yaml::events` with checks off is at most 1.5x the instructions of saphyr-parser on `large`, `deep` and `scalars`.
- Any row still above that is explained in the README by a named, profiled cause, and filed as its own issue.
- All outputs stay byte-identical to the Rust programs', and the package's tests and the yaml-test-suite pass list are green.

# Issue #1555: Integers say whether a step overflowed and give a product's high half (overflowing_*, widening_mul)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1555).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-10 · updated 2026-11-10 · 0 comments

## Why

ADR-270 D11 (corrected by the owner, 2026-11-10): a wider number than `i64` is taken only for a measured reason. Where a product may leave the range, the means is a method that says whether it overflowed and gives the high half, not an `i128` or a big integer. `std` has `checked_*` and `wrapping_*` (Part I, 10-nikaia-light.md:401-410, 557) and nothing that gives both halves of a product or the wrapped result with its overflow flag.

## Decision (supervisor, obvious extension by the language principles)

Two method families on every integer type, by the names readers know from the `wrapping_`/`checked_` family:

* `overflowing_add/sub/mul(b)` returns `(wrapped result, bool overflowed)`;
* `widening_mul(b)` returns `(low, high)`: the low half as the unsigned type of the same width, the high half as the type itself, so `high * 2^w + low` is the exact product.

## To build

1. Part I: the names beside `checked_*` (one paragraph, the result shapes above).
2. `std`: the methods in Nikaia (`crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/*.nika` or the std source where `checked_mul` lives); no new Rust beyond what the lowering writes.
3. Prover: the facts each result gives (`!overflowed` implies result = exact value; `high == 0 && low <= MAX` implies the product fits), so code that tests the flag is proved like a `checked_*` guard.
4. Tests in `tests/compiler/`: `i64::MAX.overflowing_add(1)` gives `(i64::MIN, true)`; `(1 << 40).widening_mul(1 << 40)` gives `(0, 1 << 16)`; a guard on the flag proves the next index.

## Done when

The four tests pass, Part I names the methods, and `--bounds` proves an index after `if !overflowed`.

# Issue #1559: Codegen: a generic handed to a bounded std method fails rustc (implied DeepSize, Eq lowers to Eq + Hash)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1559).

`ready`, `safety` · opened 2026-11-10 · updated 2026-11-10 · 2 comments

Filed by the driver from the `Found:` of the run of `issue-1544` (#1544) (owner, 2026-11-06).

## Found

A std method whose Rust impl needs a trait bound fails rustc on a generic:
- `fn forward[T](tx: channel::Sender[T], x: T) { tx.send(x) }` gives NK1343 "`T: DeepSize` not satisfied". This is the bound #1540 put on `impl Sender<T>`; `SharedMut::set` and `join` behave the same.
- `fn put[T](mut s: ref collections::HashSet[T], x: T) { s.insert(x) }` gives NK1343 "`T: Eq`, `T: Hash`".

Ledger signatures carry no bound (ADR-024 D9 writes `?`), so the checker does not ask for one and the emitter does not add one.

## Decision (supervisor, 2026-11-10)

1. **`DeepSize` is implied.** The language weighs every value: the runtime has `DeepSize` for every type a program builds, and a closure is weighed through `Kept`. So no Nikaia bound is written for it. Where a generic body hands a `T` to a std operation that weighs it, the emitter writes `T: nikaia_std::block::DeepSize` on that parameter. It does the same on the parameter of every generic caller that passes its own type parameter there. Recorded in ADR-327, added under D9.
2. **A map key or set element needs `[T: Eq]`.** A key is compared, so a type parameter used as one needs `[T: Eq]` as `==` does. Without it the call is refused with NK1248, not passed to rustc. Every `Eq` type hashes (NK1260), so the bound lowers to Rust's `Eq + Hash`. Recorded in Part II, beside the `Hash` trait.

## To build

- [ ] Reproduce both Found probes (`nikaia run scripts/probe.nika -- SNIPPET`).
- [ ] Emitter (`.nika`): infer `T: DeepSize` from the std calls in a generic body that weigh a `T` (the operations whose Rust impl carries `DeepSize`: `Sender::send`, `SharedMut::set`, task join/result), and carry it through generic callers to a fixed point.
- [ ] Checker: a type parameter passed as a key or element to a hashed collection without `[T: Eq]` (or `Ord`) gives NK1248.
- [ ] Emitter: an `Eq` bound on a type parameter lowers to `Eq + std::hash::Hash`.
- [ ] Tests in `tests/compiler/`: generic forward over a channel (runs); a generic caller of it (runs); `put[T: Eq]` into a HashSet (runs); `put[T]` without a bound (NK1248).

## Done when

Both probes compile and run as written (with `[T: Eq]` for the set), the unbounded set probe gives NK1248, and the tests are green.

# Issue #1560: grammar: a rule's values are lent, not cloned per call (ADR-grammar-1 D6)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1560).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-10 · updated 2026-11-10 · 2 comments

**Decision (supervisor, 2026-11-10):** ADR-grammar-1 D6. D2 already makes a rule's values a function's parameters, so ADR-views-3 D1-D4 hold for them:
- the caller writes nothing, and a plain value is lent;
- `keep` keeps it;
- `ref` is refused (views-3 D4).

Today the lowering clones every rule value at every call. On the yaml package's large input, `List<Dir>::clone_in` is 4 % of all instructions (cause 2 of #1548).

**Probe** (`ref` refused today with NK1102; the plain form clones per call):

```nika
struct D { h: String }
grammar G {
	rule WS = "" -> { }
	entry rule top -> i64 =
		ds:Dir+ ";" v:Two(ds) -> { v }
		| ";" v:Two([]) -> { v }
	rule Dir -> D = "%" s:text("a"+) -> { D { h: s } }
	rule Two(ds: Vec[D]) -> i64 = a:Item(ds) b:Item(ds) -> { a + b }
	rule Item(ds: Vec[D]) -> i64 = "x" -> { ds.len() }
}
fn main() throws {
	println(G::top("%a%aa;xx") catch { return })   // 4
	println(G::top(";xx") catch { return })        // 0
}
```

**To build**
1. `check_grammar` (`grammar_value`): a rule value takes the views-3 parameter forms. Plain means lent, and `keep` and `mut` are accepted where a function accepts them. `ref` is refused with the code and message a function parameter gets.
2. `emit_pattern_call` and the grammar lowering pass a lent value to the engine as a borrow, with no `.clone()`. A literal argument (`Two([])`) is held in a temporary that lives for the call.
3. The engine, winnow-grammar codegen `rule.rs:50` (where the clone is written), takes the borrowed form. If the engine cannot express it, open a winnow-grammar PR and bump its rev.
4. Tests in `tests/compiler/`:
   - the probe above, printing 4 and 0;
   - `ref` on a rule value refused;
   - a test that the lowered Rust holds no clone of a lent rule value, if the existing test forms can say it.
5. Re-measure the yaml package with callgrind (`benches/yaml/README.md` method) and update the table.

**Done when** the probe prints `4` and `0`, no rule value is cloned per call in the lowered yaml package, and the yaml figures in `benches/yaml/README.md` are re-measured.

# Issue #1562: A type parameter used as a hash key needs `[T: Hash]` (ADR-010 D13); a literal handed to a generic bound to String reaches rustc as `&'static str`

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1562).

`ready`, `safety` · opened 2026-11-10 · updated 2026-11-11 · 0 comments

Filed by the driver from the `Found:` of the run of `issue-1559` (#1559). The supervisor decided it on 2026-11-11 as [ADR-010 D13](../blob/develop/docs/specification/adr/adr-010.md).

## What this is, from zero

A `HashMap` key and a `HashSet` element need Rust's `Hash + Eq`.
- **Declared types.** ADR-010 D11 already decides this: a declared type hashes from its fields, or by its `impl Hash` when it has an `impl Eq` (D12). That build is #591.
- **Type parameters.** This issue builds the rule for a type parameter in that position: it must be bounded by `Hash`, and `Hash` includes `Eq`.

```nika
fn count[T: Hash](xs: List[T]) -> collections::HashMap[T, i64] { ... }   // builds
fn bad[T: Eq](xs: List[T]) -> collections::HashSet[T] { ... }           // NK1248, names [T: Hash]
```

Today the second form reaches rustc with `T: Hash`. #1559 added NK1248 for a fully unbounded hashed key. Its item (c), lowering `Eq` to `Eq + Hash`, is rejected by D13: a type with its own `impl Eq` and no `impl Hash` would fail every `[T: Eq]`. `tests/language` `std_bounds` already passes such a type.

## Found (from #1559)

1. A concrete struct used as a `HashSet` element or a `HashMap` key fails rustc with `P: Hash`, because no emitted struct derives `Hash`. This is #591, and is built there.
2. Take `relay(ty, "eight")`, where `relay[T]` binds `T = String` from a `Sender[String]`. The literal is passed as `&'static str`, so rustc reports a mismatch (NK1343). This is a separate lowering defect: a literal handed to a parameter whose type is bound to `String` is converted with `.to_string()`.

## Cause

Traced in #1559's run:
- the bound list in the checker (ADR-341 D1) has no `Hash`;
- `emit_function` lowers a bound by name;
- the generic literal conversion does not look at the substituted `T`. This last point is suspected, not traced.

## To build

1. **`Hash` is a standard bound.** `[T: Hash]` is accepted, gives the body `==`, and lowers to `T: ::core::hash::Hash + Eq`. A bound is answered by the D11 walk or by an `impl Hash`; until #591 lands, only the language's own types answer it. Test: `tests/compiler/tests/hash_bound.nika` and its `.stdout`, with a `count[T: Hash]` over `i64` and `String`.
2. **A type parameter in a hashed position without `Hash` is `NK1248`.** The hashed positions are:
   - a `HashMap` key;
   - a `HashSet` element;
   - an argument to a parameter so bounded, including `[T: Eq]` alone.

   The message names `[T: Hash]`. This replaces #1559's unbounded-only check. Test: `tests/compiler/tests/hash_bound_missing.nika` and its `.stderr`.
3. **A literal handed to a generic parameter bound to `String` is lowered as an owned `String`.** This is Found 2. Test: `tests/compiler/tests/generic_literal_string.nika` and its `.stdout`, using #1559's `relay` probe.
4. **Specification.** Update Part III's list of standard bounds and the NK1248 entry, and add one sentence to Part I wherever `Eq` and `Ord` are named as bounds.

## Files and limits

- Files: `check_*.nika` (the bound list), `emit_function.nika`, the generic call lowering, and the lowered files they write.
- Do not change #591's derive of `Hash` for declared types. That is its own build.
- No version, CHANGELOG or badge changes.

`[T: Hash]` builds a hash map over `T`, `[T: Eq]` in a hashed position is NK1248 naming `[T: Hash]`, `relay(ty, "eight")` builds, and the three tests are green at `--both-settings`.

use std::io

fn month_name(month: int) -> String {

Every index on a value parsed from a request, standard input, a file or a database row.

# Issue #1573: A request's query, header and body are not outside data to NK1202 and NK1302

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1573).

`ready`, `safety` · opened 2026-11-11 · updated 2026-11-11 · 0 comments

Found by the builder of #1572 (NK1302, ADR-396).

## Probe

```nika
// an http::listen handler (examples/http)
fn handle(request: Request) -> Response {
    let names = ["red", "green", "blue"]
    let at = text::parse_i64(request.query("color") ?? "0") ?? 0
    return Response::text(names[at])          // expected NK1302, gets NK1207/NK1300
}
```

An `assert` on `request.query(...)` gives `NK1300`, not `NK1202`.

## Why it is a defect

ADR-010 D2 classifies an `http` request line, its headers, query and body, and `net` sockets as **untrusted**. ADR-010 D1 says that a value computed from an untrusted one is untrusted. `Request` gets its bytes from a socket (`provenance = "untrusted"` in `std.contracts`). Somewhere between the socket read, the struct field and the method's result, the flow drops that provenance:

- In one package, the walk should follow it through a field and through a function result whose body it reads (ADR-396 D1: "through every call whose body it reads in the package").
- Across a package's boundary, a `pub` function's result should carry it in the package's ledger, the way `std.contracts` writes `provenance = "untrusted"` for its sources.

Supervisor decision (2026-11-11), an obvious extension by the language principles: `nikaia describe` / the ledger writes `provenance = "untrusted"` for a `pub` function whose result depends on an untrusted source, and the caller's walk reads it, as it reads std's. This does not decide ADR-396 §4 (a `pub` function's own index on a parameter).

## To build

- [ ] Reproduce the probe in one package, and across a package boundary.
- [ ] Carry provenance through a struct field and a function's result in the walk that feeds NK1202 and NK1302.
- [ ] Write `provenance = "untrusted"` into a package's ledger for a `pub` function whose result depends on an untrusted source, and read it at the call.
- [ ] Tests in `tests/compiler/`: an index on a `query` result is NK1302, an `assert` on it is NK1202, and a guard on it proves the index.
- [ ] Sweep `examples/` and `packages/` with the new flow. Each NK1302 site that appears is repaired or gets a visible guard, in the same batch (ADR-396 D4).

## Done when

The probe gives NK1302 with the source named, and our own code builds.

# Issue #1576: Decision: must a `pub` function state its preconditions where its body needs a fact about a parameter? (the open package boundary of ADR-396 §4)

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1576).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-12 · updated 2026-11-14 · 1 comment

## Where this comes from

An outside consultancy made suggestions to the owner on 2026-11-12. This is one of them: *preconditions and postconditions are mandatory on public functions only, and optional inside*, said to give Vera's advantage (every function carries its contract) without its cost (writing one for every helper). The proof, with a run-time check where the proof fails, stays the mechanism. The same question is already left open in [ADR-396](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-396.md) §4, *Across a package's boundary*.

## The question, from zero

A precondition is what a function needs from its caller, for example "`i` is below `xs.len()`". In Nikaia a precondition is an `assert` about a parameter ([ADR-269](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-269.md) D4, D5). The compiler proves it at each call where it can, and checks it at run time where it cannot.

Inside one package, the compiler sees every caller. A private function's preconditions are derived from its callers, so nobody writes them ([ADR-391](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-391.md)). A `pub` function is different, because it cannot see who calls it. Its contract is the set of `assert`s its author wrote. Those are published in the ledger as `requires` and `ensures` (ADR-269 D18). The function gets two entries, one checked and one proved (ADR-269 D20). A derived precondition is never published (ADR-391 D4).

So today a `pub` function may publish no contract at all. Take `pub fn at(xs: ref Vec[int], i: int) -> int { return xs[i] }`. Nothing tells the caller that `i` must be in range. The index is checked at run time, and the call stops the program when `i` is out of range. ADR-396 refuses an index that outside data reaches and the build does not prove (`NK1302`). It leaves open whether a `pub` function's index on its own parameter counts as reached by outside data, and so needs a written precondition or a guard.

**The question:** should a `pub` function have to state, as a written precondition or as a guard, every fact about a parameter that its body needs and does not prove? Should the same go for postconditions?

## What is already decided

* Written `assert`s on a `pub` function are published and are checked at the boundary (ADR-269 D18, D20).
* A contract that changes in the breaking direction warns its author (ADR-269 D19).
* Private preconditions are derived, never written and never published (ADR-391 D3, D4).
* Across a package, a summary is only a hint, `NK1263` ([ADR-359](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-359.md) D4).
* An unproved `assert` is refused unless the build says `warn` ([ADR-380](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-380.md)).
* An index reached by outside data is proved or refused ([ADR-396](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-396.md) D1). The `pub` boundary is not decided (§4).

## How others do it

These facts are from memory, not checked.

| Language | Rule | Cost |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Vera | every function carries `requires` and `ensures` | the author writes a contract for every helper |
| Dafny | contracts are optional, but a call proves only what the callee's contract says, so in practice every function called across a proof has one | contracts on helpers too |
| SPARK (Ada) | contracts are optional. At the "silver" level every run-time check is proved, so preconditions appear wherever a check needs one | written on any subprogram whose checks need them |
| Eiffel | contracts are optional and checked at run time; a library's contracts are its documentation | none enforced |
| Rust | no contracts; a `pub fn` documents its panics in prose (`# Panics`) | nothing is checked |

## Options

1. **Do nothing.** A `pub` function's contract stays whatever its author wrote. An unproved index or division inside it is checked at run time.
   * For: no new burden.
   * Against: a library's caller cannot see from the ledger what makes a call stop. ADR-396 §4 stays open.
2. **Every `pub` function writes pre- and postconditions** (the suggestion, read literally).
   * For: every public entry carries a contract.
   * Against: most `pub` functions have nothing to claim. Mandatory postconditions mostly restate the body. It goes against "whoever uses something pays for it".
3. **A `pub` function must state what its body needs** (the narrow form). Take an index, a divisor or an overflow on a parameter that the body does not prove from its own guards. It needs a written precondition on that parameter or a guard in the body; otherwise it is refused, under `unproved-claims` as `NK1302` is. Postconditions stay optional.
   * For: the contract a caller needs is exactly the one required, and nothing else. It closes ADR-396 §4 with the rule ADR-396 already uses inside a package.
   * Against: existing `pub` functions in `std` and `packages/` will need preconditions or guards. The count is not known yet.
4. **Publish the derived precondition of a `pub` function**, so nobody writes it.
   * For: no writing.
   * Against: ADR-391 D4 rejects it. A derived contract changes whenever the body changes, so it is no promise.

## Recommendation

Option 3, with a count first. As ADR-396 D4 did, count the sites in `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools`, `packages/` and `examples/` that it would refuse, and switch it on once our own code builds under it. Postconditions stay optional: a caller who needs a fact about a result already gets the hint `NK1263` (ADR-359 D4).

## What it touches

* ADR-396 §4 (the open point), ADR-269 D5, D18-D20, ADR-391 D4, ADR-359 D4.
* The bounds walk and its report: `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/bounds_*.nika`, `--asserts` and `--bounds`.
* `std.contracts` and the `pub` functions of `packages/`, which may need preconditions or guards.
* Related: #1572 (`NK1302`, ADR-396 build), and the divisor/overflow half of ADR-396 §4 (filed alongside).

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-11-14](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1576#issuecomment-6883194089)

#### Decision (owner, 2026-11-14): option 3

A `pub` function must state a precondition, or guard the operation itself, for any index, divisor or overflow on a parameter that its body does not prove safe. Otherwise it gets `NK1302` under `unproved-claims`. Postconditions stay optional.

This is a question of correctness. The rollout is done carefully, the same way as #1578:
1. The rule is fixed. ADR-396 §4 is amended to say so.
2. The affected sites in `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools`, `packages/` and `examples/` are listed. This only decides the order of the work. It does not reopen the rule.
3. Where the prover is too weak or facts are missing, the facts are added or the prover is improved. No guard goes into our own code only so that the prover gets through.
4. The refusal is switched on once our own code builds with it.

# Issue #1577: Decision: should the compiler prove that functions and loops terminate (a guessed decreasing measure, `decreases` only where the guess fails, endless loops marked)?

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1577).

`decision` · opened 2026-11-12 · updated 2026-11-12 · 0 comments

## Where this comes from

An outside consultancy made suggestions to the owner on 2026-11-12. This is one of them: *Dafny's termination proof, but with the measure guessed automatically, a `decreases` clause written only where the guess fails, and loops meant to run forever marked explicitly.* No ADR and no issue covers termination yet.

## The question, from zero

A program **terminates** when every call returns and every loop ends. Today the Nikaia compiler proves facts about values: indexes, divisors, overflow and asserts (ADR-269, ADR-306, ADR-395, ADR-396). It proves nothing about whether a loop or a recursion ends. A `while` whose condition never turns false, or a recursion that never reaches its base case, builds without complaint and hangs at run time.

The usual proof of termination is a **measure**: a number that is never negative and that every loop iteration or recursive call makes smaller, such as `xs.len() - i`, or `n` in `f(n - 1)`. Such a number cannot shrink forever, so the loop ends. Dafny asks for the measure in a `decreases` clause, and guesses it for simple cases.

**The question:** should Nikaia prove termination? If so, how is the measure found? Where is a `decreases` written? How is a loop marked that is meant to run forever, such as a server loop, an event loop or a task that waits on a channel? And what happens to a function the prover cannot show to terminate: refused, a warning, or only reported?

## What exists that it builds on

* [ADR-361](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-361.md): loop invariants are found automatically (Horn clauses, PDR, and proposals from a language model that the prover then checks). Nobody writes an invariant. A measure could be found by the same machinery: a ranking function is one more candidate to check.
* [ADR-276](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-276.md): `while true` is the one unconditional loop. That is already a visible mark for "meant to run forever".
* [ADR-321](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-321.md) D7: code run at build time has a step budget of ten billion steps. That is a run-time guard, not a proof.
* [ADR-269](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-269.md) D10: the prover is incomplete on purpose, and what it cannot prove falls back to a run-time check. Termination has no run-time check to fall back to, which is why this needs its own decision.
* #1435 (the compiler derives "deterministic"): a proof of termination would be a natural sibling property in the ledger.

## How others do it

These facts are from memory, not checked.

| Language | Rule |
| :--- | :--- |
| Dafny | every loop and recursion must terminate. A `decreases` measure is guessed (the parameters in order, or the loop bound) and written where the guess fails. `decreases *` marks a method that may run forever, and it can only be called from other `decreases *` methods |
| Lean, Agda, Idris | total by default. Structural recursion is accepted automatically, others need a well-founded measure. `partial` (Lean) and `covering` (Idris) mark the rest |
| F* | `Tot` versus `Div` effects: a function that may diverge says so in its type |
| Vera | contracts on every function. Whether it proves termination is unknown to me |
| AILANG, Boruna, Mojo | no termination proof that I know of |
| Rust, Go | none. `loop {}` marks the intended endless loop, but nothing proves the others end |

## Options

1. **Do nothing.** Termination is not proved, and hangs are found by tests.
   * For: no work, and no false refusals.
   * Against: a hang in a library is invisible in its contract.
2. **Report only.** The compiler tries a measure (guessed, or found as in ADR-361). `--bounds` / `--asserts`, or a new `--termination`, lists each loop and recursion as proved to end, meant to run forever (`while true`), or unknown. Nothing is refused.
   * For: cheap, it tells the author where the risk is, and it gives a count to decide on.
   * Against: nothing enforces it.
3. **Proved or marked, refused otherwise (Dafny's rule with a guessed measure).** Each loop and recursion is proved to end by a guessed measure, has a written `decreases`, or is marked as endless (`while true`, or a function-level mark that spreads to its callers like Dafny's `decreases *`). Otherwise the build refuses it under `unproved-claims`.
   * For: termination becomes part of the contract, and an AI author gets one more fact checked.
   * Against: new syntax (`decreases`, a function mark). Some code the prover cannot handle needs a written measure, for example loops on data read from outside, or `while` loops over a linked structure. The count is unknown.
4. **Only for build-time code and for functions claimed `deterministic` or pure.** Terminating is required where it matters most, for `meta` and comptime code and for #1435's derived properties, and reported elsewhere.
   * For: smaller blast radius, and it replaces the step budget's guesswork where a proof is found.
   * Against: two rules.

## Recommendation

Option 2 first, then decide between 3 and 4 on the count. Build the measure search on ADR-361's machinery: a ranking function is checked like an invariant. Treat `while true` as the existing endless mark, so no new keyword is needed for it. Take a `decreases` keyword and a function-level "may not terminate" mark only if the count shows the guess fails often enough to need them.

## What it touches

* ADR-361 (the invariant search would also search for measures), ADR-276 (`while true` as the endless mark), ADR-321 D7 (the build-time step budget), ADR-269 D10.
* The prover and the bounds walk (`crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/bounds_*.nika`), and a report flag in Part III (`30-nikaia-tooling.md`).
* Grammar, if `decreases` or a function mark is taken.
* The ledger (ADR-292), if "terminates" becomes a published property next to #1435's.

# Issue #1578: Decision: refuse a divisor or an overflow reached by outside data the way an index is refused (ADR-396 §4), and list `/` and `%` in `--bounds`

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1578).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-12 · updated 2026-11-14 · 1 comment

## Where this comes from

An outside consultancy made suggestions to the owner on 2026-11-12. This is one of them: *safe arithmetic, with division by zero and overflow either proved impossible or handled explicitly, never silently wrapping and never `x / 0 = 0`.* Most of this is already decided in Nikaia. This issue files only the part that is missing.

## The question, from zero

Integer arithmetic has two run-time failures: **overflow**, where the result does not fit the type, and **division by zero**, which covers `/` and `%`. Languages pick among wrapping silently (C for unsigned values, Go), defining `x / 0` as `0` (Pony, some verification languages), stopping the program, or proving at build time that the failure cannot happen.

Nikaia already stops the program on both, and drops the check where it is proved. For **indexes**, [ADR-396](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-396.md) goes one step further: an index that data from outside the program reaches, and that the build does not prove, is refused (`NK1302`, #1572). ADR-396 §4 leaves open whether a **divisor** and an **overflow** reached by outside data are refused the same way. It says this "waits on the count".

A second, smaller gap is the report. `nikaia build --bounds` (#389) lists each index and each `+`, `-` and `*` as proved or checked. It does not list `/` or `%`, so an author cannot see which divisions still carry a check.

**The question:** should a divisor or an arithmetic operation that outside data reaches, and that the build does not prove safe, be refused like an index? And should `--bounds` list `/` and `%`?

## What is already decided (and is not reopened here)

* Overflow aborts the program ([ADR-285](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-285.md) D5). There are no wrapping operators: wrapping, saturating and checked arithmetic are named functions, not operators like `&+`, which ADR-285 D6 rejected ([ADR-315](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-315.md)).
* There is no `x / 0 = 0`. Division by zero is unrecoverable at run time (Part I, `10-nikaia-light.md`). A constant zero divisor is `NK1118`, and `checked_div` gives `null`.
* A check is dropped where it is proved ([ADR-306](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-306.md)).
* A divisor shown to be zero is refused (`NK1207`), and the divisor check is never dropped silently ([ADR-395](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-395.md) D1-D3).
* An index on outside data is proved or refused (ADR-396 D1, `NK1302`, #1572).

## How others do it

These facts are from memory, not checked.

| Language | Overflow | Division by zero |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Rust | panics in debug builds, wraps in release builds unless configured | panics |
| Swift | traps; `&+` wraps | traps |
| Zig | undefined behaviour in release-fast builds, checked in safe builds | the same |
| SPARK | proved absent at the "silver" level, or refused | proved absent, or refused |
| Dafny | mathematical integers with no overflow; machine types need proofs | the divisor must be proved non-zero (a precondition of `/`) |
| Pony | wraps | `x / 0 = 0` |
| Vera, AILANG, Boruna | not known to me |

## Options

1. **Do nothing.** Divisions and overflows stay checked at run time where they are not proved, and `--bounds` keeps silent on `/` and `%`.
   * For: no new refusals.
   * Against: outside data can stop the program through a division where it cannot through an index, and the report hides it.
2. **Report only.** `--bounds` lists `/` and `%` as proved or checked, with what reaches the divisor, as it does for `+`, `-` and `*`. Nothing new is refused.
   * For: small, and it gives ADR-396 §4 its count.
   * Against: closes only the visibility gap.
3. **Report, then refuse on outside data (ADR-396's rule extended).** As option 2. After a count over `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools`, `packages/` and `examples/`, an unproved divisor or overflow that outside data reaches is refused with a code next to `NK1302`, under `unproved-claims`. The author fixes it with a guard, a `checked_*` call or a precondition.
   * For: one rule for all three run-time failures on outside data. It is exactly the consultancy's "proved or handled".
   * Against: overflow on outside data is common, for example sizes from a file or sums of read numbers, so the count may be large. It needs the range analysis to be good enough.
4. **Refuse divisors only, report overflow.** A divisor is rarely legitimately unguarded, while overflow is everywhere.
   * For: a smaller blast radius.
   * Against: two rules.

## Recommendation

Option 2 now. It is small: `bounds_report_checked_op` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/bounds_report.nika` returns true only for `Add`, `Sub` and `Mul`, so it can take `Div` and `Rem` as well, and Part III's `--bounds` text needs the matching change. Then decide between 3 and 4 on the count that option 2 gives, as ADR-396 D4 did for indexes.

## What it touches

* ADR-396 §4 (second bullet, the open point), ADR-395 D1-D3, ADR-285 D5-D6, ADR-306.
* `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/bounds_report.nika` (`bounds_report_checked_op`), and the bounds walk.
* Part III `30-nikaia-tooling.md` (`--bounds`), plus a new NK code next to `NK1302` if option 3 or 4 is taken (to be reserved by the supervisor).
* Related: #1572 (`NK1302`), #1567, #682, #632, #1053, and the public-function half of ADR-396 §4 (#1576).

## Comments

### keywan-ghadami, [2026-11-14](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1578#issuecomment-6883193435)

#### Decision (owner, 2026-11-14)

This is a question of correctness, not of a count. **The rule for indexes in ADR-396 applies the same way to `/`, `%` and overflow of `+`, `-` and `*`.** An operation that outside data reaches, and that the build does not prove safe, is refused, with a code next to `NK1302` under `unproved-claims`.

**Overflow:** the rule applies only to the plain operators. Where the author has chosen how overflow is handled, for example with `wrapping_*`, `saturating_*` or `checked_*`, that choice is the handling and nothing is refused. Only a plain `+`, `-` or `*` that is not proved safe on outside data is refused.

**Rollout, done carefully, because the prover is not yet strong enough in many places:**
1. The rule is fixed. ADR-396 §4 is amended to say so.
2. `--bounds` lists `/` and `%` as proved or checked, as it already does for `+`, `-` and `*` (`bounds_report_checked_op` in `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/bounds_report.nika`, and Part III `30-nikaia-tooling.md`).
3. Where the prover is too weak or facts are missing, the facts are added (std contracts, ledger entries) or the prover is improved. No guard goes into our own code only so that the prover gets through.
4. The refusal is switched on once our own code (`crates/nikaia-std/src/tools`, `packages/`, `examples/`) builds with it.

#### To build

* The ADR-396 §4 text, and a new NK code reserved by the supervisor.
* The `--bounds` report for `/` and `%`, with a test in `tests/compiler/`.
* The prover and fact work that step 3 finds, each gap as its own issue.
* The refusal behind `unproved-claims`, with tests: refused on outside data, accepted when proved, and accepted with `wrapping_*`, `saturating_*` or `checked_*`.

# Issue #1579: Decision: should Nikaia import and call Python modules (the direction ADR-284 does not cover)?

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1579).

`decision` · opened 2026-11-12 · updated 2026-11-12 · 0 comments

## Where this comes from

An outside consultancy made suggestions to the owner on 2026-11-12. This is one of them: *Python interoperability as Mojo has it, so that the Python ecosystem (numpy, pandas, ML libraries) is usable from Nikaia from day one.* Half of this is decided. This issue files only the other half.

## The question, from zero

Interoperability with Python has two directions:

* **Python calls Nikaia.** A Nikaia library is used from a Python program. This is **decided**: [ADR-284](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-284.md) D26-D27. A package built with `artifact = "c-library"` exports a C ABI, and `nikaia bind python` generates a `ctypes` binding over it. ADR-284 §2 rejected PyO3-style native extension modules, one per language. Open work is in #112 and #88.
* **Nikaia calls Python.** A Nikaia program imports a Python module, for example `numpy`, and calls its functions with Nikaia values. **Nothing covers this.** Foreign code reaches Nikaia only from Rust crates ([ADR-290](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-290.md), [ADR-393](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-393.md)) and through the C ABI.

Calling Python means embedding the CPython interpreter in the Nikaia process, or talking to a separate Python process. It brings dynamic types into a statically typed program, reference counting and Python's global interpreter lock across the boundary, and a run-time dependency on an installed Python.

**The question:** should Nikaia offer calling into Python? If so, in what form: an embedded interpreter, a separate process, or only through the C ABI that already exists? And under which permission?

## What exists that it builds on

* ADR-284 D26-D27: the C library artifact, and `nikaia bind python` for the other direction.
* ADR-290 and ADR-393: using Rust crates. These are the model for a foreign dependency in `nikaia.toml`.
* #1433: the permission vocabulary. Embedding CPython is `native` (foreign code that the compiler cannot see), and a separate Python process is `process`. Either way, the caller's package has to be granted it (#1434).
* The ownership model: Nikaia has no garbage collector, so a Python object held from Nikaia needs a handle type that owns one reference count.

## How others do it

These facts are from memory, not checked.

| Language | How it calls Python |
| :--- | :--- |
| Mojo | embeds CPython. `Python.import_module("numpy")` returns a `PythonObject`, a dynamically typed handle, and calls go through the interpreter at Python speed |
| Julia | PythonCall.jl / PyCall.jl embed CPython, and values are converted or wrapped |
| Rust | PyO3 can embed an interpreter as well as build extension modules. Calls return `PyResult` and need the GIL token |
| Swift | PythonKit (formerly in Swift for TensorFlow), dynamic member lookup over an embedded CPython |
| AILANG, Boruna, Vera, Dafny | no Python calls that I know of. Dafny compiles *to* Python instead |

## Options

1. **Do nothing.** Python code is reached only by running it as a process (`std.process`, permission `process`), or by wrapping it in C.
   * For: no dynamic types in the language, no CPython dependency, and nothing for the permission proof to treat as opaque.
   * Against: the ML and data ecosystem is out of reach, and that is the ecosystem an AI-written program most often needs.
2. **A package that embeds CPython** (Mojo's model) with a `PyObject` handle type. Values are converted at the boundary (int, float, str, list and dict as `std` types) and errors come back as `Result`. It is a package in `packages/`, not part of the language, and it needs the `native` permission.
   * For: the whole Python ecosystem. No grammar change. It is opt-in and visible in the permission grants.
   * Against: dynamic calls the prover cannot see into, a CPython ABI to follow across versions, and the GIL. In the spirit of "no new Rust", it needs C-ABI calls from Nikaia (ADR-290/393 cover Rust crates, not arbitrary C libraries). That may be a gap of its own.
3. **Typed bindings generated from Python stubs** (`.pyi` files or `typing` annotations). A tool reads a module's stubs and writes a typed Nikaia facade over option 2's handle.
   * For: static types at the call site, and AI-friendly.
   * Against: stubs are often missing or wrong, and it is more work.
4. **A separate Python process with a typed message protocol.**
   * For: no CPython in the process and a clean failure boundary. Permission `process`.
   * Against: slow for numeric work, and every value is copied.

## Recommendation

Option 1 for now. Write down in ADR-284 that the reverse direction is not provided and why, and come back to option 2, as a package and never as language syntax, once calling C libraries from Nikaia is decided. The consultancy's "from day one" argument is about the ecosystem's reach. Weigh it against keeping the permission and proof story whole: an embedded interpreter is one large `native` hole.

## What it touches

* ADR-284 (D26-D27, §2), ADR-290 and ADR-393 (foreign dependencies), #1433 and #1434 (`native` / `process` permissions), #112 and #88 (the decided direction).
* If option 2 or 3 is taken: a new package in `packages/`, how Nikaia calls a C library (possibly a gap to decide first), and the ownership of foreign handles.

# Issue #1580: Decision: a record-and-replay mode that records every outside input of a run and replays it deterministically

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1580).

`decision` · opened 2026-11-12 · updated 2026-11-12 · 0 comments

## Where this comes from

An outside consultancy made suggestions to the owner on 2026-11-12. This is one of them: *a replay mode that records all effects of a run (file reads, network answers, clock, random numbers, AI calls) so that any run, including a failure in production, can be replayed exactly, for debugging and for audit.* No ADR and no issue covers it.

## The question, from zero

A program run is reproducible when the same code given the same inputs does the same thing. Most runs are not reproducible, because they read things from outside: the clock, random numbers, files, the network, environment variables, standard input, and the order in which tasks are scheduled. A bug that shows up once in production may never show up again on the developer's machine.

**Record and replay** fixes this. In record mode the runtime writes every value that comes in from outside to a log. In replay mode it reads them back from the log instead of from the world, so the run repeats exactly, step for step. This makes a production failure reproducible, a test of the failure a matter of keeping its log, and an audit able to show exactly what a program saw.

**The question:** should Nikaia offer a record-and-replay mode? If so, at which boundary are inputs recorded, how is concurrency made replayable, and what is promised: an exact replay, or a best effort?

## What exists that it builds on

* #1433: the permission vocabulary (`file`, `net`, `stdin`, `args`, `env`, `clock(wall)`, `clock(mono)`, `random`, `process`, `native`, ...). Every way in which outside data enters a program already has a named kind, and a call that reads outside data goes through `std` under that kind. **That is exactly the boundary to record.** A program whose permissions are proved (#1432) cannot read the world any other way, except through `native`.
* #1435: the compiler derives "deterministic" and "can measure time". A function that is deterministic needs nothing recorded. Only the permissioned calls do.
* The task scheduler (async, #983): the order in which tasks run is an input too. It must be recorded or made deterministic.
* [ADR-010](../blob/main/docs/specification/adr/adr-010.md) (provenance): a recorded log is a provenance record of a run.

## How others do it

These facts are from memory, not checked.

| System | How |
| :--- | :--- |
| rr (Mozilla) | records a Linux process at the system-call level and replays it under a debugger, with reverse execution. It works for any language, but runs on one core and needs hardware counters |
| Boruna | records effects in an audit log as part of its capability model (as far as I know) |
| Temporal, Azure Durable Functions | workflow code must be deterministic. Every side effect is an "activity" whose result is recorded and replayed when the workflow resumes |
| Elm | the time-travelling debugger replays the messages of a pure program |
| Haskell, Koka, Unison | effect handlers make swapping the real world for a recorded one a library matter |
| AILANG | describes deterministic replay of effects as a goal (not verified) |
| Vera, Dafny, Mojo | none that I know of |

## Options

1. **Do nothing.** Reproduce bugs with logs and tests, or use rr outside the language.
   * For: no work, and rr already exists on Linux.
   * Against: rr is Linux-only and debugger-oriented, with no audit log and no test from a recording. It does not use the permission boundary Nikaia already has.
2. **Record and replay in `std`, at the permission boundary.** `nikaia run --record LOG` makes every `std` call that reads outside data (by the #1433 kinds) append its result to the log. `nikaia run --replay LOG` returns the values from the log instead. With tasks, the scheduler records its order, or runs single-threaded and deterministic under replay. A program using `native` cannot be replayed exactly, and the tool says so.
   * For: it uses the boundary #1432/#1433 already prove complete. It works on every platform. A log can become a regression test (`nikaia test` from a recording). An AI call is `net`, so it is recorded like any other answer.
   * Against: runtime work in every input path of `std`, and the log may hold secrets (environment variables, network answers), so it needs a redaction story. The scheduler's order has to be pinned.
3. **Replay for tests only.** A recorded run turns into a fixture, and `nikaia test` replays it. There is no production record mode.
   * For: smaller, and still makes failures reproducible once caught.
   * Against: does not catch the production failure that started the wish.
4. **Leave it to effect handlers.** If Nikaia ever has user-definable effect handlers, replay becomes a library.
   * For: general.
   * Against: Nikaia has permissions, not effect handlers, and this would be a far larger decision.

## Recommendation

Option 2, scoped after #1433 is built, because it needs the vocabulary to name what to record. Promise an exact replay only for programs without `native`, and with the scheduler pinned. Treat the log as sensitive by default: no environment variables recorded unless asked, and a redaction hook. Ship option 3 (a recording as a test fixture) as its first user.

## What it touches

* #1432 and #1433 (the permission kinds as the recording boundary), #1435 (deterministic functions need no recording), #983 (async scheduler order), ADR-010 (provenance).
* `std`'s input paths (file, net, clock, random, env, args, stdin, process), the task runtime, and the `nikaia run` / `nikaia test` commands in Part III (`30-nikaia-tooling.md`).
* A log format, and where it sits next to the ledger (ADR-292).

# Issue #1581: A cold lowering of the tools package takes 3–5 minutes, most of it in the bounds walk and the prover

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1581).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-14 · updated 2026-11-14 · 0 comments

Part of the CI-speed work (owner, 2026-11-14: CI in 1–2 minutes, not 40–70).

## What is slow

A cold `nikaia lower-std` takes **2.5–3 minutes** on 4 cores, and **5.5 minutes** in the builder cycle. `docs/builder-facts.md` and `builder.md` still say about 40 s (181 G instructions). "Cold" happens every time the compiler binary changes, because the lowering cache is keyed on the binary's hash. So it happens:

* in every builder cycle after a Rust or `tools/*.nika` change;
* in CI, once per whole-tree test that lowers the tools package. After the changes on `ci/speed` there are three such lowerings: `the_committed_rust_is_what_this_compiler_lowers`, `map_trust::the_real_tools_package_lowers_the_same_read_backwards`, and `the_tools_lower_the_same_on_one_thread_as_on_every_core`. They set the floor of the CI run at roughly 5–7 minutes.

Measured on 2026-11-14, on a 4-core cloud container, with the `fast` profile:

* `lower-std`: real 5m30s, user 10m48s in the builder cycle. A salted cold run on a sysroot copy (`NIKAIA_LOWER_CACHE_SALT`, `--sysroot` copy) took about 3 minutes.
* `map_trust` backward, one lowering at `tools_build()` on every core: 317 s.

## Where the time goes (8 `gdb` samples of all threads during a cold `lower-std`)

The frames that appear in the stacks most often:

* `bounds_proven` 33
* `bounds_walk::bounding_stmts` / `bounding_stmt` / `bounding_block` 20 / 18 / 17
* `prover_arena` 19
* `bounding_expr` 9
* `proofs_answers::proofs_search` / `proofs_ask` 7 / 7
* `sv_ask` 6, `lg_search` 6, `ledger_infer_package` 6, `rules_check` 5

At the top of the stacks there is no single hot spot. The time is spread over `malloc`/`free`, the drop glue of `Ty` and `BTreeMap<Text, i64>`, `List::from_array` in `SvTseitin`, and `memcpy` in `modules_call_starts`: allocation and copying throughout the walk and the solver.

## Done when

A cold `lower-std` on 4 cores takes **under 60 s** again, measured as `docs/measuring.md` asks: callgrind instructions, against the 181 G recorded in `builder.md`.

## To build

1. Measure with callgrind, per `docs/measuring.md`: count the instructions of a cold `lower-std` and attribute them per function. Record where the growth from 181 G came from. `git log` of `bounds_*.nika` / `prover_*.nika` / `sv_*.nika` since the 40 s figure is the place to start.
2. Remove the copying in the hot path: the clones of `Ty` and of the facts maps per statement in `bounding_stmts`, and `List` allocations in `SvTseitin`. Each one is its own commit, with the instruction count before and after.
3. Decide (this is a `decision` question if it is not obvious): should the **proof results** be cached per function, keyed on what determines them? That is the function's source, the ledger entries it reads and a version of the prover rules, instead of the compiler binary's hash. A compiler change that does not touch the prover would then re-prove nothing. `docs/ci-cache.md` notes the same idea for the `lower-std` cache.

## Files and limits

`crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/bounds_*.nika`, `prover_*.nika`, `proofs_*.nika`, `sv_*.nika`, `logic_*.nika`. Nothing in this issue may change a verdict: `lower-std` output and every `.bounds` expectation stay byte-identical.

## Ruled out

* Parallelising the tests that lower the tools: they already lower on every core.
* Restoring the lowering cache in CI: its key is the binary's hash, which every commit moves.

# Issue #1582: nikaia test's batch build: lower a program as a module in the emitter, and lower the batch on every core

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1582).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-14 · updated 2026-11-14 · 0 comments

Part of the CI-speed work (owner, 2026-11-14). It follows the batch build on `ci/speed` (`project_batch.nika`, commit "nikaia test builds a package's test programs once per setting").

## Where it stands

Since that change, `nikaia test` builds the test programs of one setting as **one crate**. The wrapper lowers every program, makes each one a module `p{k}`, adds a dispatcher `main` and runs one `rustc`. A program the batch leaves out, or whose batched run fails or writes to standard error, is built alone as before, and that run decides the test. For tests/compiler at one setting, 943 of the 1242 programs that lower go into one batch. In CI the batch build takes **74–146 s per shard**.

Two parts of it are stopgaps:

1. **The module is made by editing text** (`project_batch_module`):
   * `crate::` becomes `crate::p{k}::`;
   * a line that starts with `enum` / `struct` / `type` gets `pub`;
   * the last line that starts `fn main(` gets `pub`;
   * the `#[global_allocator]` line is dropped.

   A program text that holds such a line is changed along with the code. The program then prints something else, its batched run fails and it is built alone, which is correct but slow. In the prototype, 15 programs had `fn main(` inside a string.
2. **The wrapper lowers the programs one after another**: 1242 × ~0.12 s ≈ 2.5 minutes on one core. Each lowering reads and checks the dependency package (`compiler_tests`) again.

## Done when

The emitter lowers a program as a module without editing text, and the batch of tests/compiler at one setting is lowered in **under 20 s** on 4 cores.

## To build

1. An emit option, "as module `NAME`", in `emit_*.nika`. Paths to the crate root are written relative to the module, the items `main`'s signature names are `pub`, and the allocator is left to the crate. `project_batch_module` then only wraps.
2. Read and check the dependency package **once** for the whole batch, not once per program: one `Open`, or a cache of the package's ledger and parse.
3. Lower the programs of a batch on every core. The wrapper process can use threads, or `project_tests_batches` can hand the wrapper lowerings already made by the workers.
4. When the batch's `rustc` fails, find the failing modules from its messages and drop them, instead of only splitting the batch in two. This is what `accepted_sweep.rs` does program by program.

## Files and limits

`crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/project_batch.nika`, `project_tests.nika`, `project_drive.nika`, `emit_*.nika`, and `crates/nikaia/src/project.rs` (host). No verdict of `nikaia test` may change: the batch only speeds a test up.

# Issue #1583: The `solver_cnf` test takes about 13 minutes and sets how long CI takes

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1583).

`ready`, `wip` · opened 2026-11-14 · updated 2026-11-14 · 3 comments

**Found while** cutting CI time (run 43587711114, commit cffb2b1e; the related issues are #1581 and #1582).

## Symptom

`tests/compiler/tests/solver_cnf.nika` runs in a CI shard of its own, `compiler-slow-solver_cnf`. Measured on run 43587711114:

* that shard takes about 12.8 minutes after the build (5.5 min);
* every other test shard is done after about 4–9 minutes;
* since the per-shard sweep (2cdd0f95), the critical path of the whole run is: build, then this shard, then the 30-second sweep check.

## Cause (traced)

`main` of the test does three things:

1. It concatenates the sources of ten tools: `prover_arena`, `solver_terms`, `prove_text`, `logic_lia` and `sv_num`, `sv_row`, `sv_proof`, `sv_check`, `sv_sat`, `sv_cnf` from `crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/`.
2. It adds the driver from its own comment lines.
3. It runs `nikaia run main.nika`.

`nikaia run` then does all of the following, cold, on a program of several thousand lines:

* the checker, including the prover;
* the lowering;
* a `rustc` build.

All of this code is already lowered and compiled in std (`crates/nikaia-std/src/tools/lowered/`). The test compiles it a second time just to call it.

Minor point: `let dir = if name == "sv_rod" { "solver" } else { "tools" }` is dead (no name is `sv_rod`).

## To build

1. Run the driver against the tools as they are already compiled, so the test no longer builds them from source. Either:
   * a test of the tools package that `nikaia test` runs against the built std; or
   * the driver as its own file, with `use` of the tools module, if the functions are reachable.

   If neither can be said in Nikaia today, that gap is a finding (CLAUDE.md, *A missing form stops the work*).

# Issue #1584: A program `nikaia run` builds in a test shard does not find `libstd-*.so` without LD_LIBRARY_PATH

[Open and answer this issue on GitHub](https://github.com/Nikaia-Foundation/Nikaia/issues/1584).

`ready` · opened 2026-11-14 · updated 2026-11-14 · 0 comments

**Found while** cutting CI time: test shards now run the prebuilt test binaries directly instead of through `cargo test` (dee80f81, cffb2b1e).

## Symptom

In CI run 4 on `ci/speed`, before dee80f81, the solver tests failed in a test shard. The program that a nested `nikaia run` had built (the fast path, `crates/nikaia/src/run_fast.rs`) would not start:

```
.../target/nikaia-project-tests/run/main-50a51e66d9cc4606/target/nikaia/fast/main: error while loading shared libraries: libstd-7d3c8b3343c9c95a.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
```

Two changes to the workflow make it pass:

* putting `$(rustc --print sysroot)/lib` and `$(rustc --print target-libdir)` on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (dee80f81), which is what `cargo test` does;
* exporting `RUSTUP_HOME`, `CARGO_HOME` and `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN` (cffb2b1e).

Both settings now stand in the `Test` step of `.github/workflows/nikaia.yml`.

Locally, in the cloud container, `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH nikaia run main.nika` runs a hello-world fine (binary of 2026-11-14, cffb2b1e). So the probe has to be the CI shard itself: remove the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` line from the `Test` step and run the `compiler-*` shards.

## Governing decision

#281: the program is `exec`ed as it is, with nothing set around it. `run_fast.rs` therefore writes an rpath for the bundle's directory, its `deps` and `bundle.libdir`. The program is meant to start without `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.

## Cause (suspected, not traced)

`bundle.libdir` (or the `libstd` the bundle dylib was linked against) comes from a different toolchain directory than the one the rpath names. One possibility: without `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`, the `rustc` lookup resolves another toolchain than the one that built the bundle. The `libstd` hash in the error should match exactly one toolchain's `lib/rustlib/<target>/lib`.

## To build

1. Reproduce in CI without the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` line. Print `readelf -d` (RUNPATH) of the failing `fast/main`, and the path of the `libstd-<hash>.so` it needs.
2. Fix the rpath, or the toolchain lookup, in the `nikaia run` fast path, with a test (if it can be said in a `tests/compiler` program; otherwise a finding).
3. Remove the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` line from the workflow.

## Done when

The test shards pass with no `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` set by the workflow, and a program built by `nikaia run` starts on any machine with the toolchain the repository names.
